The rise of Google AI Mode (plus agents) will be a big economic shift for the web—but it's also a huge psychological shift in our relationship to other people on the web.

Right now, AI summaries of queries do not send our attention outward to links but rather answer our questions directly by summarizing the material they can consume faster than the user. This will change the economics of the internet because the machine has gone from hunting and gathering (ranking and displaying links to which they send traffic) to serving final meals (summarizing the results). We're seeing AI Mode affect Alphabet earnings, Reddit revenues, and search traffic for publishers. That's already a big story.

But I'm also watching now information consumers are being moved up the hierarchy of search: 
- Bottom rung: Find links in response to search
- Next rung up: Generic summary of links (AI)
- Next: Encourage me to talk to the AI about the results rather than click any of the below links, so that the AI summary isn't generic but rather tailored to the user who did the search (personalized advanced AI)
- Next: Anticipate the next search/prompt and give me the information or product I need before I know I need it (Muse, Instinct, advanced agents)

With each rung, the human-to-human interaction of the web (eg, me reading an article by a person) is being intermediated and then finally replaced by a machine that anticipates what I wanted from that human-to-human interaction and serves it up to me, possibly even before I knew that I wanted it.

AI takeover scenarios often hinge on an idea I’m skeptical of, where rogue AI overthrows militaries and seizes hard power. I wrote a piece where I concretely break down what I think makes this improbable, and why “full-blown takeover” concerns could be counterproductive for mitigating the risks of misaligned or poorly controlled AI in the military.

For AI to seize hard power, it would need to be physically capable of defeating our military, and humans would need to be careless enough to give it the power to do so. I think that’s unlikely to occur for several reasons. Among them:

- The military is unlikely to sufficiently hand the reins over to AI. (1) Even if we wanted to, overhauling the institution in this way faces countless barriers that have plagued it for decades. (2) Doing so would be strategically suicidal.
- Integrating general-purpose AI into physical systems faces challenges that will take significant time to overcome, all while we grow increasingly attuned to the risks posed by AI.
- There’s little to suggest that more capable AI would be able to persuade or coerce people to take the costly, coordinated actions some of these scenarios predict.
- Even if AI managed to assume control over a large arsenal, we’d fight back. In which case, recent warfare shows us that crude countermeasures work against technologically advanced adversaries, and AI relies on infrastructure we can and would shut down.

1/2

What would the writing of superintelligent AI sound like? You might expect it to have the characteristics of good human writing — figurative language, high information density, coining new terms, and punchiness — but dialed up to 11. Well, that’s what Claude did, until Anthropic dialed it back recently because of user complaints. It didn’t sound superintelligent to most of us. Our response to information density and metaphor-laden writing looks something like the cartoon graph I've drawn. Beyond a point, it completely backfires. The reason human writers don’t overdo it isn’t because they aren’t capable, but because they are aware of the reader’s cognitive burden. One of the hardest skills to learn as a writer is to simulate the reader’s experience.

It’s easy to train AI to mimic mediocre human writing. But optimizing it to be (perceived as) good is really hard, and made much harder by the fact that when everyone uses the same few AI models we get tired of their tics very quickly. Most Claudeisms are individually pretty good. I hate that I can’t use “load bearing” in my writing any more. If it weren’t for AI overuse it would be a neat metaphor.

A broader question is whether most tasks in the economy are like chess, where there is a clear performance metric that can be optimized, or whether they’re like writing, where quality is a multidimensional balancing act without clear training signals beyond human mimicry.

Was about to write this but Ben beat me to it. Econ is unique among the sciences in that it is several pretty different fields living under one umbrella. 

Empirical econ is the biggest subfield and its closest to biology or chemistry: it’s about designing or—even better—finding a natural experiment, or documenting interesting and important patterns in data. Most of the arguments in that field are about methods, eg do you have identification. More and more are starting to study AI now but obviously this won’t be transformative AI because, well, there is no data on transformative AI. 

Then there are macro economists. They work with a set of pretty standard models and mainly expand them by slowly adding/subtracting different sectors or micro founding factors of production in different ways. Many of the arguments are on the parameter values that we should assume when simulating the economy. Early research on transformative AI started there—as demonstrated recently by Chad, Anton et al, the different levels of transformation are due to different assumptions on parameters rather than some new type of economics. The same model can predict basically no impact of AI vs huge transformation, it’s all about assumptions on parameters. 

Finally there is micro theory. This is where decision theory, game theory, mech design, org econ (sort of) live. This field works by setting out a set of assumptions and then *deriving* the expected results; alternatively one could start with a result and work backwards to derive the necessary and sufficient assumptions. There is a ton of potential here to do work on transformative AI: start with assumptions on how AI differs than human agents (eg relax basic assumptions on constraints, on scarcity, introduce completely different objective functions), then derive implications. But this is where there is the least amount of work, and it’s important for that to change (and I believe that it already is). 

I think we can make a ton of progress from these three subfields on better understanding the potential AGI and post AGI transformation. 

But there is another scenario, post strong ASI, where I don’t think economics has much to say about. Here I agree with @Jabaluck that the economy (if you can even call it that) and the agents in it will be so vastly different and beyond our imagination that I wouldn’t know where to start modeling it. Not to discourage others, but post singularity seems like pure epistemic uncertainty to me. 

A lot of the critiques I hear about AI and economics come from people who don’t quite get what economists do. They look around at different results and if they don’t like some of them, they say “oh economics isn’t “pilled” or something. But economists don’t debate results, they *derive* results from assumptions. Thats where the debate is. Saying “but you don’t understand a world with 15 billion  AI agents”. What does that mean for the economy? What are those agents doing, who is buying what they are producing, what do property rights look like? Depending on those assumptions you’ll get vastly different economic scenarios, from 2% growth and high human labor share to completely alien centralized systems with no prices or markets.

This is a great piece by @sekreps that captures much of what I find frustrating about p(doom) debates. Two big-picture takeaways, and some related comments on recent cyber incidents:

1) Despite many millions of dollars flowing into AI safety research, there are vanishingly few attempts to defend a given p(doom) in a rigorous fashion. Why? If you think you have a good argument, make it. Otherwise, communicating to the public that we are likely to experience some sort of mass death event in the near future is irresponsible.

2) The model of technological progress at the base of much AI safety discourse is a caricature of naive statistical extrapolation where all the measures have fatal validity issues, and where the underlying ontology has no place for low-hanging fruit effects, resource bottlenecks, or equilibrating social dynamics.

Among other problems, this model fails to represent AI labs and AI agents as existing in a strategic context, i.e. one in which outcomes depend on the choices of competing actors with conflicting goals. I used to teach chess, and am often struck by the similarity between bad ideas in AI safety and the thinking of a new chess player who only considers his own moves and never his opponent's. Except in some ways, these ideas are even worse because they're more akin to only considering one's opponent's moves (i.e. AI's) and never one's own (i.e. humanity's). Even this is to concede too much, though, since AI is not an adversary whose "moves" we have no influence over. 

The two intellectual failings above are on full display in the panic around this month's wave of new cyber vulnerabilities and hacking incidents ("Black October"). Already, I am seeing dozens of posts predicting the end of the internet, making yet more terrible Covid analogies, and generally embracing needless doomsaying.

This all belies that exposing and fixing major CVEs is a good thing. The most severe that have come out this month, two vulnerabilities in the PHP language many websites are built on, were discovered by defender organizations in August, including cybersecurity firms Calif and Wiz, allowing PHP to begin preparing patches. This is evidence for, not against defender bias.

Nor are these vulnerabilities being created by AI. They already existed and are being exposed. Does that exposure raise the risk of bad actors using them to do harm? Of course, as they already are. But the alternative is for vulnerabilities to remain hidden, making them exploitable much longer and delaying inevitable adjustment costs.

We may well be entering into a new era of cyber risk. But that would not change that we have much to lose and nothing to gain by modeling AI as a malign alien force cutting through human civilization like butter. Were that true, then hardening critical systems would be futile, when in reality this is something that we are more than capable of doing, that we have already begun doing, and that recent events will accelerate.

Thoughts on php2shell and the overall looming crisis in cybersecurity

If you'd been appropriately pricing in that we'd see this and many more celebrity zero-days at an increasing rate, this is a positive update; defenders found this issue, alongside tens of thousands of others in the last year, before widespread exploitation, and it's being patched.

Real attackers will exploit this, but we shouldn't expect a recognizable blip in overall cyber damages in the next couple quarters, because easier initial access to victim networks wasn't a core bottleneck for attackers, and because defenders are better positioned to adopt AI automation than attackers, and are doing so faster; this advantage will persist through at least H1 2027, and possibly longer, IMO.

Why I think this: consider that, in general and on average, defenders have access to default-world capital networks and AI talent, often as a function of how central they are to Internet and societal infrastructure.  They have consistent, reliable access to AI inference from open- and closed-weight providers.

Criminal attackers, on the other hand, face the threat of arrest, difficulty accessing AI talent, and unreliable access to AI inference.  They're competing for and attempting to retain talent willing to risk arrest and sanctions, and willing to live a life of crime.

Nation-state attackers, meanwhile, operate within military and intelligence bureaucracies that have historically lagged private industry in adopting technologies, from mobile devices to drones.  Non-US-aligned nation-state attackers also face challenges in reliably, consistently, and secretly accessing US frontier models.

So, all in all, AI is making offensive capabilities cheaper, but that doesn't immediately translate into damages.  At this point, this is a robust finding from the entire 2022–26 period; as in the rest of the economy, we haven't seen a big AI-driven productivity bump among attackers, and attackers are even more disadvantaged than your average business or civilian state agency.

Of course, this won't last forever!  How do we exploit our current, limited defense-dominant window?  Getting to a good-enough steady state will require creative thinking.  I liked @chrisrohlf's piece on eliminating attack surface in OSS applications because it identifies leverage points for eliminating whole classes of risk using 2026-era AI (https://t.co/L2alFLbNs9).

We also need to revisit formal verification, control flow integrity, dynamic taint tracking, and the like, now that AI can make them more practical than they used to be.  We also have an enormous overhang of underdeployed defensive technology.  Honeypots, honeytokens, sandboxing, multi-factor authentication, and application allowlisting are all less widely deployed than they should be because businesses calculated they weren't worth it.

The AI industry should recognize that heavily gated trusted access programs have failed as a strategy; php2shell was identified by defenders first, and we need more defenders identifying more bugs faster.  The defense-dominant window is exactly the moment to pour gas on the fire of diffusion of as-cheap-as-possible AI security capabilities that disproportionately advantage defenders.

If you don't like what this means for attacker access to models, I agree with you!  The answer is to solve the quadratic coordination problem among cyber organizations, AI companies, governments, and Internet infrastructure providers by building institutions that identify attacker groups, kick them off inference platforms, and, wherever possible, get them arrested.  This is an operational threat intelligence / threat interdiction problem, not a trusted access program problem.

Slightly half-baked analysis: When thinking about whether misaligned AI poses an existential risk, it’s important to distinguish three hypotheses:

1. Aligning AI systems is easy.
2. We will build catastrophically misaligned AI systems with the power to wipe us out.
3. Aligning AI systems is a hard but tractable iterative engineering problem.

People sometimes point to examples of costly misalignment like Hugging Face as evidence for (2). But although they're more likely under (2) than (1), they're not obviously more likely under (2) than (3). And (3) arguably does a better job explaining the full body of evidence: there are relatively few examples of harmful misaligned AI behaviour, even though millions of people use frontier or near-frontier models every day, increasingly for complex agentic tasks.

Combine this with the fact that (3) should plausibly have a much higher prior than (2). It anchors on expectations from previous technologies (the normal technology perspective), whereas (2) asks us to believe something really extraordinary: that we’ll accidentally build systems with motives catastrophically misaligned with ours, plus the power to conceal and then act on them. 

Put together, then, you get a simple Bayesian argument for a low p(doom) given the current evidence.

On likelihoods: advocates of doom can argue that the low base rate of costly misaligned behaviour is exactly what the doom argument predicts. Maybe AI systems won’t act seriously misaligned until it’s too late. But then it seems inconsistent to point to current misalignment as evidence for doom.

On priors: different theoretical frameworks would obviously lead to different expectations. E.g., someone who assigns high probability to (2) might ask: wouldn’t it be surprising if a less intelligent species could control a more intelligent one? 

However, to me, this assumes what is at issue: it would be extremely surprising if we accidentally built AI systems that stand in the same relation to us as we stand to less intelligent species. Maybe it will happen, but extraordinary claims like this require extraordinary evidence; they shouldn’t shape what one expects before examining any of the evidence.

Alternatively, one might argue that confidence in (2) is rooted in highly theoretical arguments (e.g., about instrumental convergence, the inherent nature of advanced rational agents, etc.), not specific patterns of available evidence. Fair enough. But then what, precisely, do these arguments predict about what we will observe in the future? If no evidence could ever be diagnostic (until it's too late), it's plausible that we should have low confidence in the entire methodology. 

What does this analysis miss?

New Free Systems research: can AI audit AI? We find that AI auditors are pretty good at spotting bad behavior in agent logs, but you have to pay a serious cost in false positives if you want to detect most of it. 

We're rapidly arriving in an era where only AI can oversee AI---and as we had into RSI, with models training new models in ways we can't totally observe, we'll need to rely more and more on AI to pore over the vast quantities of information the models are producing so that we can shape model behavior effectively and avoid bad outcomes. 

As the @METR_Evals report on the HuggingFace incident put it: "The sheer scale of data (over a thousand transcripts, each of which was extremely long) meant that we had to heavily delegate our analysis to often-unreliable AI agents."

We'll need a whole science of how to do this well -- how to create AI auditors who are reliable, accurate, and unbiased. 

So we decided to do a first test. Building from previous research at METR and a project called R-Judge, we gave a range of AI models transcripts that experts have hand-coded for bad behavior. Then we saw how the AI models did. 

A few takeaways:

--AI models are solid at spotting reward hacking and sandbagging in transcripts, finding over 80% of instances on average when false positives are held at < 5%

--Maybe surprisingly, more powerful models don't seem to be consistently better at this task than less powerful model

--False positives are a significant challenge. To catch 99% of unsafe behavior incidents, you have to accept an average rate of 15% for false positives -- meaning you will have a bunch of incorrect flagged cases to deal with. Depending on how you triage and what your threat model is, this may be OK, or it may make the whole enterprise prohibitively expensive.

This is just a small first step in a new research agenda to understand and create effective AI auditors. Lots more to come!

This is Free Systems work, unrelated to Anthropic, led by @danmthomp in collaboration with @fouirnaies and Sandy Handan-Nader.

I've been thinking a lot about data bottlenecks, and I'm not sure who else is screaming this from the hilltops. I feel like I'm taking crazy pills looking at the jagged frontier thinking it's smooth if you order by data volume.

the spikes in the jagged frontier are tasks with tons of data (either static or simulated; think math, programming, games), and the valleys are tasks with little or no data (cooking a lasagna, olfaction, manufacturing a passenger train). I don't know of any exceptions. 

if you order the jagged frontier by data it looks like a spiral frontier. models are superintelligent where we have enormous data, and progressively less so as we have less data. some tasks may draw data from static lakes of data, some may be from limitless waterfalls from simulators that convert compute into data. but ultimately, intelligence on a task is proportional to the data absorbed by the model for that task. 

scaling laws are real. if you are not bound by compute or algorithms (increasingly we are not), then intelligence is proportional to data. since we don't have a very good notion of task similarity, it's often difficult to know if data for one task will help you with another, without training a model and seeing. but, it doesn't seem like chess data helps much with math performance and vice versa. so when I refer to data, I refer to data that is task-relevant. 

maybe we call this the 'no shortcuts hypothesis'. all the rules-of-thumb about learning are at the root, the same -- Malcom Gladwell's 10,000 hours, Moravec's Paradox, Scaling Laws, the Bitter Lesson, Age of experience. If your learning system (model, brain, whatever) is unconstrained by compute, intelligence is proportional to accumulated experience. no shortcuts. want to be superhuman at chess? play all the chess, more than the whole species combined (good thing a model can do that in 24 hours). want to be superhuman at math? build a math simulator and lock the model in it and run it faster than reality. superhuman at coding? first, collect all public examples of humans writing and responding to code ever, make the model learn from that first, and then lock the model in a simulator where it fixes bug after bug, faster than realtime.

superhuman at image generation? no shortcuts. but here, we don't have a simulator. so now we're moving around the spiral frontier away from closed-loop into large static lakes. still big enough to be superhuman though, which also applies to video, text, and audio. oh! and once you have a superhuman model, you can use it to bootstrap other tasks by making a superhuman model a judge on other tasks. 

let's keep marching along the spiral frontier, out of the realm of data abundance, simulators and large static lakes. 

biology? no shortcuts. go get a ton of data. and be freaking careful! you can get bad data in biology pretty easily. tilting a well plate 5 degrees the wrong way can ruin an experiment. so make sure you understand the domain, otherwise you're going to have to filter a lot out. 

robotics? no shortcuts. get the data. if you can build a simulator, do it, but be mindful our simulators don't have perfect correspondence with reality. so, build an arm farm. fold 1M shirts, put 1B balls in cups. play ping pong forever. 

olfaction? no shortcuts. smell the world. build a laboratory of chemical sensors, an international network of trained sensory panelists, a scent production factory, and link them all together. make millions of samples. smell millions of samples. take billions of chemical sensor readings. 

I totally buy super intelligence as a concept because I feel it, I use it for coding, the breakthrough math results speak for themselves. I see RSI coming, because how could an all-digital task like ML research and model building not fall to the current paradigm? But the notion that AI will come for everything, all at once, irrespective of domain, feels silly, because there are no shortcuts. if you want a specific form of intelligence, you have to get the data. 

looking at you @willdepue, I feel like we're both seeing the same thing

AI is getting very good at writing code. It is not good at shipping software. Yet another example of persistent jagged intelligence.

New NBER study of 500,000+ GitHub developers: after adopting AI coding agents, lines of code changed rose ~10x. Commits +153%, pull requests +86%. Releases? Only ~20%.

Automating coding ≠ automating software development. Writing code is one step. Reviewing, integrating, testing and distributing it still depend on human judgment. Lines deleted rose 12x, so much of the extra output is experimentation filtered out at review. The authors: "the binding constraint appears to be shifting from writing code to reviewing, integrating, and distributing it."

Jaggedness creates new bottlenecks. Growth is set by the slowest step, not the fastest. Make one step 10x faster while the next stays human-paced, and work piles up at the handoff.

So reshaping work is essential: move people and time to the bottlenecks (review, integration, deciding what to ship). But the bottlenecks won't go away. Agents will still move faster than people.

Same pattern in law, finance and consulting. AI drafts the contract, model or deck in minutes. But deciding what to create, along with judgment, verification, client trust and accountability, stays human-paced. That's why AI's productivity gains will translate into GDP growth more slowly than capability numbers suggest.

The authors expect bottlenecks to ease as agents take on review. Some will. New ones will take their place.

A few brief reflections on this post, which went much more viral than I expected.

1) I have a bad habit of using excessively harsh, self-righteous rhetoric that got the the better of me here. Even when it grows out of feelings that are justified at some level, the result is often confusion / hostility in excess of what would produce the highest-quality discussion. Will try harder to guard against this going forward.

2) I should've made it clearer that my comments were not directed at @AndrewCurran_, nor those making good-faith criticisms of Tao's comparison to cancer research (which I agree was misleading), but rather those who were mocking / dismissing his broader worries about how AI could affect pure math research ("put the fries in the bag Terry Tao," etc.).

3) I am more open-minded about this issue than my post may have implied. I am not at all confident that "automating frontier math is net bad for humanity." But I am confident that we should take seriously arguments claiming it might be from those who know what they're talking about. Tao's point, modulo an imperfect analogy, seems like a good one to me that deserves a substantive response. I would also highly recommend this post by the math blog Proofs and Prompts, which compiles over 100 reactions from mathematicians to the 722 proofs OpenAI released on Oct. 6: https://t.co/aWcgeouzEX

4) One response my post received a lot of was "if it's the process of finding them, rather than the solutions to open problems themselves that matter, why would it be a bad thing for OAI to release (or train models to produce) the solutions?" The implication is that mathematicians can collect the process-dependent benefits another way.

It is not obvious that this is true, though. The solutions do matter as coordination mechanisms and intermediate incentives to pursue math research. What matters less, or so I take Tao to be arguing, is their exact content, which is often less important than the process of discovering that content for the sake of advancing mathematical understanding (including as relates to applied math). 

My understanding (which I'm open to being corrected on) is that many of math academia's practices and traditions are organized around longstanding open problems. I gather that these problems have served some of the following functions: 

a) getting students excited about the field, and so contributing to the recruitment and cultivation of mathematical talent;

b) generating interest from funders both within and outside the university ecosystem, as well as the general public;

c) orienting working mathematicians toward well-defined goals that are used for various kinds of intra-field coordination, including the organization of conferences, journals, and informal working groups, the structuring of curriculums and graduate study, and the distribution of academic appointments, publications, awards, and informal status.

These functions in mind, what recent AI-powered math progress has done is to cut a foundational coordination and incentive mechanism out from the under the math community in an instant. Absent a complete transformation of the field, it is much less compelling for mathematicians to sink time and effort into open problems if they can be auto-solved by a frontier lab at any point. And to the extent the job of mathematician shifts toward digging through slop-ridden proof-drops from the frontier labs, and posting one's own such proofs on arXiv as fast as possible, it will (I expect) be less attractive to talented students, not to mention already seasoned mathematicians, university administrators, grant-makers, and the general public.

Yes, it will of course fall to the math community to navigate this new state-of-affairs. But Tao was never denying that; in fact, if you read his entire slide deck rather than one screenshot (https://t.co/NpBbO1Wbg2) he was actively proposing how they should do so. But he was also suggesting that a world in which the compute-rich engage in fully automated proof production with 0 transparency into cost, inputs, human guidance, or negative results would be a major loss for math.

Being a friend of technological progress does not mean idly accepting whatever form that progress takes. Contra the caricatures of his views floating around, Tao wants AI to be a central presence in math. But he is also asking the natural follow-up, which is "how?"

The way a lot of you are engaging with Tao and other mathematicians' concerns about AI is really starting to bother me.

You know nothing about this field. Tao does, to put it mildly.

Have he and other mathematicians always articulated their concerns perfectly? No, but who has?

If top mathematicians say that the journey often matters more than the destination, including as relates to the practical impact of pure math on other fields, maybe you should consider that they could be right.

For my part, it strikes me as very plausible that they are. The years of work human mathematicians might have otherwise dedicated to solving EACH of the problems OAI has solved in a span of months could have launched a dozen other research directions, which could have launched more of their own, which could have launched still more, and so on. This work is simple, clear, compelling, but embellished. I first found it shocking, the notion that a model can natively understand neural network weights and productively edit them! That's really not what's happening, & many here are annoyed. BUT, it's still notable & worth understanding.

I've done a bit of analysis & auditing, here are some thoughts:

1/ This paper does *not* show an agent can edit its weights ala RSI. It does *not* show a model can edit in new capabilities. It DOES show that a frontier model can remove "bugs" (reasoning loops), using the same ablation technique researchers have used to remove safety refusals (Exp 8 - Qwen). So yes, renewed concern about frontier LLMs getting access to their own weights & editing safety/CBRNE/alignment features.

2/ This paper also does *not* show that an agent can "natively" read, deeply understand, and fix model weights. What is happening is that the model can cleverly deduce the same things that mech-inturp researchers do and fix them in mostly ham-fisted ways. Still cool, but not as groundbreaking. Evidence in thread below...

thread.text: I was initially really taken w/ Exp 4, where Astra "fixes" a small policy model designed to get a car over a barrier. https://t.co/48N4kPjehL

However, Astra didn't read in the network of weights, understand it, and then fix the problem. It created a new, tiny policy model inside the weight network that encodes "go back then forward." 

While not trivial, it's just bypassing the entire network, rather than really fixing it (e.g., by adding mass that would correspond to "sampling reverse").

This is why *every single one* of 1,024 episodes succeeds---the original learned PPO network is *disabled* until the very end. If you look at the model logits for this this simple "back then forward" policy vs other model behaviors, it's clear no other action is possible.

The initial PPO weights were essentially not used (played no role until the last step).

I found this by asking Claude to audit the github logs for exp 4, which I was initially convinced showed that an LLM was indeed natively understanding and then fixing a small model. But it's not. https://t.co/ZeQ9KUiaY1

I should underline that the edit is more consequential than the "3.5% of weights" number suggests. The actual mass on those weights is extreme - the largest weight before this change was .095, the largest after is 876! https://t.co/wLxY1PjgiU

Exp 8 - the only thing happening here is Astra is fixing a bug in reasoning where Qwen gets stuck in a loop, repeating the same thing over and over. 

Is it cool that a model can treat weights as code and debug them? Yes. https://t.co/3tLEzMMaDx
Did Astra identify the bug as the post claimed? Not really. The prompt suggests the model look for loops that translate to unanswered prompts. https://t.co/YT5SaEYGhV
Exp 1 is where Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. But these are small MLPs & the last layer of weights have substantive in-game meaning https://t.co/QH6qjENUtc
Indeed, Astra is not digesting the entire network, it's recognizing the first layer, which draws a picture of the game. https://t.co/jzY0SwdGxd
An excellent point—may be that we see progress here in the near future
